items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to limiting the duration of a conditional appointment and to amend chapter 147 of the laws of 2001, amending the education law relating to conditional appointment of school district, charter school or BOCES employees, in relation to extending the effectiveness thereof
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5765

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the education law, in relation to limiting the
duration of a conditional appointment and to amend chapter 147 of the
laws of 2001, amending the education law relating to conditional
appointment of school district, charter school or BOCES employees, in
relation to extending the effectiveness thereof


 PURPOSE OF THE BILL :

To extend the ability of school districts, charter schools, and Boards
of Cooperative Educational Services (BOCES) to make conditional
appointments of prospective employees under certain necessary
conditions and to limit the duration of a conditional appointment.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of the bill would amend paragraph (b) of subdivision 39 of
section 1604 of the Education Law to provide that the conditional
clearance for prospective employees of common school districts would
terminate forty-five days after notification by the Commissioner of
such conditional clearance and could not be extended or renewed unless
a new conditional clearance is issued after a finding that the
employee demonstrated good cause for failing to obtain clearance
within the initial forty-five day period.

§2 of the bill would amend paragraph (b) of subdivision 39 of section
1709 of the Education Law to permit prospective employees of a union
free school district to be issued a conditional clearance, which would
terminate forty-five days after notification by the Commissioner of
such conditional clearance. Such conditional clearance could not be
extended or renewed after the initial forty-five day period unless the
applicant had demonstrated good cause for failing to obtain clearance
within the initial thirty day period.

§3 of the bill would amend paragraph (b) of subdivision 9 of section
1804 of the Education Law to permit potential employees of a central
school district to be issued a conditional clearance, which would
terminate forty-five days after notification by the Commissioner of
such conditional clearance. Such conditional clearance could not be
extended or renewed after the initial forty-five day period unless the
applicant had demonstrated good cause for failing to obtain clearance
within the initial thirty day period.

§4 of the bill would amend subparagraph (b) of paragraph 11 of
subdivision 4 of section 1950 of the Education Law to permit a
prospective employee of a BOCES to be issued a conditional clearance,
which would terminate forty-five days after notification by the
Commissioner of such conditional clearance. Such conditional clearance
could not be extended or renewed after the initial forty-five day
period unless the applicant had demonstrated good cause for failing to
obtain clearance within the initial thirty day period.

§5 of the bill would amend paragraph (b) of subdivision 18 of section
2503 of the Education Law to permit a prospective employee of a small
city school district to be issued a conditional clearance, which would
terminate forty-five days after notification by the Commissioner of
such conditional clearance. Such conditional clearance could not be
extended or renewed after the initial forty-five day period unless the
applicant had demonstrated good cause for failing to obtain clearance
within the initial thirty day period.


§6 of the bill would. amend paragraph (b) of subdivision 25 of section
2554 of the Education Law to permit a prospective employee of a large
city school district (other than the New York City school district,
which conducts its own criminal history record checks) to be issued a
conditional clearance, which would terminate forty-five days after
notification by the Commissioner of such conditional clearance. Such
conditional clearance could not be extended or renewed after the
initial forty-five day period unless the applicant had demonstrated
good cause for failing to obtain clearance within the initial thirty
day period.

§ 7 of the bill would amend subparagraph (ii) of paragraph (a-2) of
subdivision 3 of section 2854 of the Education Law to permit a
prospective employee of a charter school to be issued a conditional
clearance, which would terminate forty-five days after notification by
the Commissioner of such conditional clearance. Such conditional
clearance could not be extended or renewed after the initial
forty-five day period unless the applicant had demonstrated good cause
for failing to obtain clearance within the initial thirty day period.

§8 of the bill would extend the date on which the provisions of
Chapter 147 of the Laws of 2001 would expire from July 1, 2009 to July
1, 2010.

§9 of the bill would provide that all conditional clearances issued by
the Commissioner of Education pursuant to sections 1604, 1709, 1804,
1950, 2503, 2554 or 2854 of the Education Law prior to the effective
date of this bill would expire forty-five days after the effective
date of July 1, 2009. Such conditional appointments would not be
extended or renewed unless the applicant demonstrates good cause for
failing to obtain clearance within this forty-five day period.

§ 10 of the bill would be the effective date.

 STATEMENT IN SUPPORT OF THE BILL :

Chapter 147 of the Laws of2001 granted school districts, charter
schools, and BOCES the authority to make conditional appointments for
certain prospective school employees. This was needed because it was
taking a longer than expected time to secure full clearances for
employment from the Commissioner of Education under Education Law
§305(30). Chapter 147 of the Laws of 2001 provided that it would be
repealed after two years, on the assumption that these delays would be
minimized and eliminated. Both Chapters 127 of the Laws of 2005 and
Chapter 90 of the Laws of 2007 extended the effectiveness of Chapter
147 for an additional two years due to the continued need for
conditional clearances.

Despite the introduction of a new interactive database (TEACH) in the
State Education Department (SED) to provide better information to
school districts, BOCES, charter schools and individual applicants
about the status of an individual's fingerprint application and the
use of fingerprint card scanning technology, SED continues to have a
backlog of fingerprint applications.  SED is implementing new
technology (LIVES CAN) to capture digital fingerprint images in the
field. This will greatly reduce the time between when fingerprints are
submitted to when the clearance for employment is issued. SED
anticipates that LIVES CAN will be increasingly available to school
districts, charter schools and BOCES. The use of LIVESCAN in
conjunction with TEACH should allow fingerprint clearance results to
be available within a few days following the transmission of the
digital fingerprint images, in most instances. There will, however,
always be situations in which clearances for employment cannot be
granted quickly. For example, the results of Division of Criminal
Justice Services (DCJS) and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
searches are sometimes delayed, a situation totally beyond SED's
control. Or, certain digital fingerprint images may contain flaws and
errors that require the applicant to be re-fingerprinted.  Such
"rejections" of fingerprint images cause additional delays in issuing
a clearance for employment. In addition, some individuals will not
have access to a digital fingerprint scan station due to their
geographic location or an employer's decision to continue submitting
fingerprint cards rather than digital fingerprint images.  Thus, the
authority for school districts, charter schools, and BOCES to make
conditional appointments is still necessary so they can meet
employment needs and the needs of their students.

If Chapter 147 were to sunset, the technical amendments relating to
teacher removal proceedings that were made by section 11 of Chapter
147 would also sunset. These amendments are necessary to make the time
frames for conducting informal conferences with teachers and building
principals following a teacher's removal of a student workable for
school districts. The amendments made· by section 11 of Chapter 147
clarify that if the 24- or 48-hour period does not expire on a school
day, it is extended to the corresponding time on the next school day.
If these provisions are not extended, a teacher would be required to
provide parents with an informal opportunity to be heard within 24
hours of a pupil's removal, even if the 24 hours expires on a Saturday
or school holiday. Similarly, building principals would be required to
offer parents the opportunity for an informal conference within 48
hours of a student's removal even if the student is removed late in
the day on a Friday or before a school vacation.

Further, this bill would provide that conditional clearances would be
valid for forty-five days. Under present law there is no time limit on
an issued conditional clearance. In February 2009 the State
Comptroller's Office issued an audit of Criminal History Background
Checks for School Employees, Report 207-S-119, in which the State
Comptroller identified a substantial number of instances in which a
background check had not been completed (469 out of 105,932
applications then pending). Of that number, 427 of the criminal
history record checks were completed, but the State Comptroller found
that the average length of time between the completion of the DCJS
background check and the final FBI check for these delayed
applications was at least eight months. This poses an unacceptable and
extended risk of students' exposure to prospective employees who may
have the types of criminal histories that could result in their
preclusion from such employment. To address this, the bill would
establish a time limit for conditional clearances.  Conditional
clearances were never intended to allow prospective employees to
continue to be employed for extended periods without completing both
the state DCJS and FBI criminal history record checks.

It is apparent from this data that there are too many instances in
which school districts, BOCES and charter schools are allowing
prospective employees to continue employment for a protracted period
without completing a full criminal history record check. There can be
significant delays in the processing of fingerprints through the FBI,
which has rigorous standards that cause more rejections of fingerprint
images than at the state level, but delays of this magnitude should
not occur with this frequency. To address this problem and reduce the
risk to students from contact with prospective employees who have not
yet obtained criminal clearance from the FBI's national registry, this
bill would impose a forty-five day maximum duration for a conditional
clearance and prohibit renewal or extension of a conditional
appointment unless the Commissioner issues a new conditional clearance
upon a showing of good cause for failing to obtain full clearance
within the initial forty-five days. For any prospective employee who
holds a conditional clearance on the effective date of this act, this
bill would provide that the conditional clearance would expire
forty-five days after the effective date and could not be extended or
renewed without a showing of good cause for the delay. Thus, delays in
processing fingerprints attributable to lack of diligence on the part
of prospective employers or their employees would not be excused, but
in those rare instances in which the delay is attributable to
processing delays at the state or federal levels, the bill would
provide a mechanism for allowing the prospective employee to continue
their employment beyond forty-five days. The vast majority of criminal
history record checks would be processed much more quickly, but in the
few instances of significant delays in the processing of fingerprints
through the FBI, there would continue to be allowable conditional
clearances of limited duration.

This bill would recommend that the sunset on conditional clearances be
extended for one year so the effectiveness of the forty-five day
limitation and an analysis of the need for additional changes in the
conditional clearance procedures could be fully assessed.

 BUDGETARY IMPLICATIONS OF THE BILL :

This bill would impose additional administrative costs on school
districts, BOCES, charter schools and the State Education Department
for processing requests for additional conditional clearances when the
forty-five day period elapses, but these costs are expected to be
minimal.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
July 1, 2009, provided that in the event it shall become a law after
such date, this act would take effect immediately and would be deemed
to have been in full force and effect on and after July 1, 2009.

summary: Limits the duration of a conditional appointment; extends the effectiveness of chapter 147 of the laws of 2001; provides that all conditional clearances issued by the commissioner of education prior to the effective date of this act shall expire 45 days after such effective date and conditional appointments of the prospective employees shall terminate; may not be extended unless a new conditional clearance is issued.
title: Limits the duration of a conditional appointment; extends the effectiveness of chapter 147 of the laws of 2001
